The arrival of a mysterious Peruvian mummy to a small English town heralds murder and a hunt for hidden Incan treasures.

Archie Hope seeks to marry the delightful Lucy Kendal, the stepdaughter of Professor Braddock, an eccentric Egyptology enthusiast. Though perhaps better known as a novelist, John Buchan was also a prolific author of short fiction, having published several short stories and collections during his life.

A Scotsman, many of Buchan’s stories are set in Scotland and feature regional folklore and customs of the region, often making use of Scottish vernacular speech. His writes in many genres, including adventure and historical fiction, and covers many themes, like spirituality and the supernatural.

A debt-ridden and conflicted landowner struggles with discontentment while his wife is dying of consumption.

The titular Ivanov is a landowner who once loved life, but is now deeply depressed and listless. His wife Anna Petrovna is a Jewish woman who was disinherited by her parents after joining the Russian Church to marry him. She’s dying of tuberculosis, and her doctor, Yevgeny Konstantinovitch Lvov, begs Ivanov to take her to Crimea to help her recover. When Ivanov refuses, Lvov begins to believe that Ivanov is a horrible man—and wants to expose him so that everyone else thinks so, too.

Meanwhile, Ivanov is deeply in debt to the wife of his good friend, the District Chairman Pavel Kirillitch Lebedyev. Despite this, Ivanov continues to thwart this estate manager’s schemes to make more money. Meanwhile Sasha, the Lebedyev’s daughter, becomes infatuated with Ivanov, and works to save him from the black cloud that is slowly enveloping him.

Some want Ivanov to be happy; others want him to be miserable. But in the end, Ivanov will choose his own fate.

Ivanov is a deep exploration of how a human being is perceived by others and themselves. As Ivanov says to Lvov: “Man is such a simple, uncomplicated machine. … No, doctor, there are too many wheels and screws and levers in any one of us for us to be able to judge each other from the first impression or from two or three external signs. I don’t understand you, you don’t understand me, and we don’t understand ourselves.”

Ivanov was first performed in 1887, but was not a success. Chekhov made changes as a result, and when it was performed again in 1889, it was much more well-received.

Original content released to the public domain via the Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication. The complete short fiction of Joseph Conrad.

Joseph Conrad, the Polish-born writer who published exclusively in English, is known as much for his short fiction as for his novels. Almost all of his stories were first serialized in periodicals such as The Pall Mall Magazine, Harper’s Magazine, and Blackwood’s Magazine. They were later republished in seven collections: Tales of Unrest, Youth: A Narrative and Two Other Stories, Typhoon and Other Stories, A Set of Six, ’Twixt Land and Sea, Within the Tides, and Tales of Hearsay. Many of his stories deal with the sea and exotic locales (the Malay Archipelago, Central Africa, South America), while others reflect his wider interests, such as his fascination with the Napoleonic era.

Conrad’s most famous novella contained in this collection, “Heart of Darkness,” was originally published serially as a three-part story. It is a short but thematically complex novella exploring colonialism, humanity, and what constitutes a savage society. Set in the Congo in Central Africa, the tale is told in the frame of the recollections of one Charles Marlow, a captain of an ivory steamer. Marlow’s search for the mysterious and powerful “first-class agent” Kurtz gives way to a nuanced and powerful commentary on the horrors of colonialism, called by some the most analyzed work at university-level instruction.

Other notable works include “An Outpost of Progress,” a precursor to “Heart of Darkness,” “Youth,” based on Conrad’s own maritime experiences, “Typhoon,” in which a stubborn captain takes on a force of nature, “The Duel,” later filmed by Ridley Scott as “The Duellists,” and “The Secret Sharer,” in which a captain harbors a fugitive. This collection comprises all the short stories and novellas from Conrad’s seven short fiction collections, plus “The Sisters,” an unfinished short story published posthumously. They’re arranged in order of first publication, which in most cases means their magazine serialization.

When three men known as the “vultures” arrive in Warsaw, princes and revolutionaries alike wonder whether they’ve come to watch for the long-awaited uprising against the Russian Empire—or to ignite it.

In The Vultures, Henry Seton Merriman plots a taut, fast-moving story of international intrigue which seems as though it could’ve been written in the modern era rather than in the Victorian.

Reginald Cartoner, a British agent, and his counterpart in the French service, Paul Deulin, have worked with and against one another for many years, building a mutual professional respect and a wary friendship. They and an American, Joseph Mangles, are known by political insiders as “vultures”—men whose sudden arrival in a seemingly peaceful place presages the end of that calm and the start of a crisis which will command the world’s attention. All three have just arrived in Warsaw, the principal city of what was formerly a free Polish state but which is now brutally controlled by the Russian Empire of Tsar Aleksandr II.

Prince Bukaty, his son Prince Martin, and his daughter Princess Wanda, whose power and wealth were stripped by the Russians decades earlier, maintain their connections throughout Europe and secretly lay the groundwork for revolt; in this they’re joined by the radical Kosmaroff, whose origins are as mysterious as his methods are ruthless. As the Polish people await the trigger for their revolution, they’re uncertain whether the three vultures have been sent to aid, to oppose, or to simply observe them, or even whether the three are cooperating or at cross-purposes with one another. As personal connections amongst all of the players are strained by conflicting duties and national loyalties, their situation in Poland becomes more perilous by the moment.

Two childhood friends—a young man who has become a renowned war correspondent and a young woman who is just emerging from the shadow of her more-celebrated sister—discover that as events conspire against them, their characters might enable them to overcome all— yet separate them forever.

Theo Trist and Brenda Gilholme have known one another since childhood. Trist has become a renowned war correspondent for influential newspapers in London and Paris, dispatched to dangerous areas of the globe to report on the most terrible events imaginable. Brenda, until now in the shadow of her sister, a celebrated society beauty, has lived the life of the mind, immersing herself in studies of languages, mathematics, theology, and political economy—a life which Victorian society doesn’t value for its daughters, but which Trist admires in the observant and analytical Brenda. Mrs. Wylie, a mutual friend who has supported each of them throughout their formative years, knows that their respective intelligence, and their senses of honor, duty, and self-sacrifice, set them apart from their peers and drive them to make the most of themselves. Those same strengths also divide and distance them from one another—and, as Mrs. Wylie knows, time is on no one’s side.

Suspense is one of Henry Seton Merriman’s more philosophical novels. In meta-commentary, the author makes plain his acceptance of Victorian views on social roles, expectations, and responsibilities, while also celebrating those who are courageous enough to stand apart from that society to live their own lives. Though an earlier of Merriman’s works, it still displays the intricate plotting, character development, and attention to place and history which are characteristic of his later works. Though its narrative and dialogue fit squarely within the framework of contemporary Victorian fiction, Suspense nevertheless demonstrates the best of that structure, even as Merriman shows with his subsequent works his desire and capability to rise above it.

Original content released to the public domain via the Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication. A proud but poor father is forced to cope with his daughter moving to the city.

Jan Andersson is a poor crofter. The only thing that brings him joy is his daughter Glory, but when the family finds itself in need of money, she moves to Stockholm to look for a job. At first Jan is despondent, especially as Glory very quickly stops sending letters. But as time goes on, Jan begins to piece together what happened to Glory in Stockholm—though his conclusions differ wildly from everyone else’s.

Blending family drama with social critique, Selma Lagerlöf explores the ways in which community and generational relations can be affected by forces both beyond and within our control, and how redemption is possible, if we so choose.

Lagerlöf considered titling the novel A Swedish King Lear, alluding to the generational conflicts central to both the novel and the play. Today The Emperor of Portugallia is considered a classic of Swedish literature, with multiple adaptations, including the now lost 1925 Hollywood film The Tower of Lies and a 1992 series for Swedish public television.

A mining engineer and his friend suffer a series of misfortunes in their search for riches and treasure.

William Thornton and Robert Seyd are two American friends who share an interest in mining. They make an agreement that whoever finds a good prospect has to contact the other so that they can work together to exploit the mine. The day to honor this pact finally comes when Robert finds a rich copper mine in Guerrero, Mexico.

On the way to the mine, William is struck by the beauty of an elegant young woman, accompanied by a large Siberian wolfhound, at a local train station. As the train approaches, the dog leaps onto the tracks. Robert, acting quickly, gets the dog to safety in the nick of time. The girl’s companion—the nephew of the general who owns the land under the mine—offers the American duo men and mules to transport their equipment to their destination.

What appears to be a stroke of good luck ends up becoming a prelude to a seemingly endless wave of challenges, as the bad omens surrounding the mine, and the general’s animosity towards Americans, threaten to lead William and Robert down a path of treachery and darkness.

https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/seneca/moral-letters-to-lucilius/richard-m-gummere Moral Letters to Lucilius Seneca https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/seneca 2026-10-16T19:00:15Z 2026-10-20T16:19:56Z Public domain in the United States. Original content released to the public domain via the Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication. An elderly Roman Stoic philosopher gives life advice to a young friend.

Seneca was a Stoic philosopher and statesman in Rome’s early post-Augustan era. He was Nero’s tutor, and then his advisor when Nero became emperor in 54 CE. After Seneca retired from public life, he wrote a series of letters to his friend Lucilius, the procurator of Sicily. These letters were circulated right before Seneca’s death in 65 CE, when Nero forced him to commit suicide for his alleged involvement in a conspiracy.

These letters, which were written for widespread publication as well as directly to Lucilius, mainly focus on guiding the reader to a life well-lived. At times, the advice is regarding specific personal issues, such as when he gives a review of a book written by Lucilius. Other letters give Seneca’s thoughts on broader issues like slavery, independence of thought, and virtue. Through all of them, his Stoicism shines through, whether in his metaphysics (like when he writes on “the god within us”) or in his focus on how virtue is the only good. His diverse interests are also on display, as when he addresses current events (like the burning of Lyons), or when he speculates on science (like when he offers his thoughts on animal instincts).

These letters have been popular and influential since their initial circulation, and were widely read from the Roman period, up through the Middle Ages, and into the Renaissance, where Michel de Montaigne used them as a model for his Essays. They remain highly regarded today for their practical and sage advice.

A domineering inventor kidnaps members of a balloonist club and flies them around the world to prove the superiority of his heavier-than-air machine.

Robur the Conqueror, also published as The Clipper of the Clouds, opens in Philadelphia at a meeting of the Weldon Institute, a club of balloon enthusiasts. A stranger named Robur asks to address the members, then tells them that the future belongs to heavier-than-air machines. He mocks the club’s giant balloon, the Go-Ahead, and insults its members until the meeting erupts in chaos. That night he kidnaps Uncle Prudent, the club’s president, Phil Evans, its secretary, and Frycollin, Prudent’s servant. He takes them captive aboard the Albatross, the flying machine he built, and flies them around the world to prove his point. After the captives escape, the story returns to Philadelphia for the first launch of the Go-Ahead, where the Albatross appears in the sky to challenge it.

First published in 1886 as Robur-le-Conquérant, this book marks the thirtieth entry in Jules Verne’s Voyages Extraordinaires. Its sequel, Master of the World, followed in 1904.

Original content released to the public domain via the Creative Commons CC0 1.0 Universal Public Domain Dedication. A young scholar’s life spirals down a dark path after the near-death of a singer.

Attending medical school in Boston, Reuel Briggs has neither wealth nor the good looks of the upper-class white society with which he surrounds himself. He is, however, incredibly talented, and has a rare gift in the psychological study of mysticism and supernatural phenomenon. Even if his peers aren’t too keen on him, they can’t help but be awed by his talent, and subsequently call on his aid in reaching out to the minds of the sick and dying who would otherwise be lost. Though this field of mysticism is his life’s work and sole talent, it may soon be his downfall as it leads him down a dark path of secrets and discoveries.

Of One Blood was first published serially in The Colored American Magazine, which Hopkins edited at the time. Written at the turn of the century and shortly after the Civil War, Hopkins explores the legacy of slavery, questions of identity, and the bounds of love and loyalty.

		<summary type="text">A debt-ridden and conflicted landowner struggles with discontentment while his wife is dying of consumption.</summary>
		<content type="html"><p>The titular Ivanov is a landowner who once loved life, but is now deeply depressed and listless. His wife Anna Petrovna is a Jewish woman who was disinherited by her parents after joining the Russian Church to marry him. She’s dying of tuberculosis, and her doctor, Yevgeny Konstantinovitch Lvov, begs Ivanov to take her to Crimea to help her recover. When Ivanov refuses, Lvov begins to believe that Ivanov is a horrible man—and wants to expose him so that everyone else thinks so, too.</p> <p>Meanwhile, Ivanov is deeply in debt to the wife of his good friend, the District Chairman Pavel Kirillitch Lebedyev. Despite this, Ivanov continues to thwart this estate manager’s schemes to make more money. Meanwhile Sasha, the Lebedyev’s daughter, becomes infatuated with Ivanov, and works to save him from the black cloud that is slowly enveloping him.</p> <p>Some want Ivanov to be happy; others want him to be miserable. But in the end, Ivanov will choose his own fate.</p> <p><i>Ivanov</i> is a deep exploration of how a human being is perceived by others and themselves. As Ivanov says to Lvov: “Man is such a simple, uncomplicated machine. … No, doctor, there are too many wheels and screws and levers in any one of us for us to be able to judge each other from the first impression or from two or three external signs. I don’t understand you, you don’t understand me, and we don’t understand ourselves.”</p> <p><i>Ivanov</i> was first performed in 1887, but was not a success. <a href="https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/anton-chekhov">Chekhov</a> made changes as a result, and when it was performed again in 1889, it was much more well-received.</p></content>

		<summary type="text">The complete short fiction of Joseph Conrad.</summary>
		<content type="html"><p><a href="https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/joseph-conrad">Joseph Conrad</a>, the Polish-born writer who published exclusively in English, is known as much for his short fiction as for his novels. Almost all of his stories were first serialized in periodicals such as <i>The Pall Mall Magazine</i>, <i>Harper’s Magazine</i>, and <i>Blackwood’s Magazine</i>. They were later republished in seven collections: <i>Tales of Unrest</i>, <i>Youth: A Narrative and Two Other Stories</i>, <i>Typhoon and Other Stories</i>, <i>A Set of Six</i>, <i>’Twixt Land and Sea</i>, <i>Within the Tides</i>, and <i>Tales of Hearsay</i>. Many of his stories deal with the sea and exotic locales (the Malay Archipelago, Central Africa, South America), while others reflect his wider interests, such as his fascination with the Napoleonic era.</p> <p>Conrad’s most famous novella contained in this collection, “Heart of Darkness,” was originally published serially as a three-part story. It is a short but thematically complex novella exploring colonialism, humanity, and what constitutes a savage society. Set in the Congo in Central Africa, the tale is told in the frame of the recollections of one Charles Marlow, a captain of an ivory steamer. Marlow’s search for the mysterious and powerful “first-class agent” Kurtz gives way to a nuanced and powerful commentary on the horrors of colonialism, called by some the most analyzed work at university-level instruction.</p> <p>Other notable works include “An Outpost of Progress,” a precursor to “Heart of Darkness,” “Youth,” based on Conrad’s own maritime experiences, “Typhoon,” in which a stubborn captain takes on a force of nature, “The Duel,” later filmed by Ridley Scott as “The Duellists,” and “The Secret Sharer,” in which a captain harbors a fugitive. This collection comprises all the short stories and novellas from Conrad’s seven short fiction collections, plus “The Sisters,” an unfinished short story published posthumously. They’re arranged in order of first publication, which in most cases means their magazine serialization.</p></content>

		<summary type="text">When three men known as the “vultures” arrive in Warsaw, princes and revolutionaries alike wonder whether they’ve come to watch for the long-awaited uprising against the Russian Empire—or to ignite it.</summary>
		<content type="html"><p>In <i>The Vultures</i>, <a href="https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/henry-seton-merriman">Henry Seton Merriman</a> plots a taut, fast-moving story of international intrigue which seems as though it could’ve been written in the modern era rather than in the Victorian.</p> <p>Reginald Cartoner, a British agent, and his counterpart in the French service, Paul Deulin, have worked with and against one another for many years, building a mutual professional respect and a wary friendship. They and an American, Joseph Mangles, are known by political insiders as “vultures”—men whose sudden arrival in a seemingly peaceful place presages the end of that calm and the start of a crisis which will command the world’s attention. All three have just arrived in Warsaw, the principal city of what was formerly a free Polish state but which is now brutally controlled by the Russian Empire of Tsar Aleksandr II.</p> <p>Prince Bukaty, his son Prince Martin, and his daughter Princess Wanda, whose power and wealth were stripped by the Russians decades earlier, maintain their connections throughout Europe and secretly lay the groundwork for revolt; in this they’re joined by the radical Kosmaroff, whose origins are as mysterious as his methods are ruthless. As the Polish people await the trigger for their revolution, they’re uncertain whether the three vultures have been sent to aid, to oppose, or to simply observe them, or even whether the three are cooperating or at cross-purposes with one another. As personal connections amongst all of the players are strained by conflicting duties and national loyalties, their situation in Poland becomes more perilous by the moment.</p></content>

		<summary type="text">Two childhood friends—a young man who has become a renowned war correspondent and a young woman who is just emerging from the shadow of her more-celebrated sister—discover that as events conspire against them, their characters might enable them to overcome all— yet separate them forever.</summary>
		<content type="html"><p>Theo Trist and Brenda Gilholme have known one another since childhood. Trist has become a renowned war correspondent for influential newspapers in London and Paris, dispatched to dangerous areas of the globe to report on the most terrible events imaginable. Brenda, until now in the shadow of her sister, a celebrated society beauty, has lived the life of the mind, immersing herself in studies of languages, mathematics, theology, and political economy—a life which Victorian society doesn’t value for its daughters, but which Trist admires in the observant and analytical Brenda. Mrs. Wylie, a mutual friend who has supported each of them throughout their formative years, knows that their respective intelligence, and their senses of honor, duty, and self-sacrifice, set them apart from their peers and drive them to make the most of themselves. Those same strengths also divide and distance them from one another—and, as Mrs. Wylie knows, time is on no one’s side.</p> <p><i>Suspense</i> is one of <a href="https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/henry-seton-merriman">Henry Seton Merriman’s</a> more philosophical novels. In meta-commentary, the author makes plain his acceptance of Victorian views on social roles, expectations, and responsibilities, while also celebrating those who are courageous enough to stand apart from that society to live their own lives. Though an earlier of Merriman’s works, it still displays the intricate plotting, character development, and attention to place and history which are characteristic of his later works. Though its narrative and dialogue fit squarely within the framework of contemporary Victorian fiction, <i>Suspense</i> nevertheless demonstrates the best of that structure, even as Merriman shows with his subsequent works his desire and capability to rise above it.</p></content>

		<summary type="text">A proud but poor father is forced to cope with his daughter moving to the city.</summary>
		<content type="html"><p>Jan Andersson is a poor crofter. The only thing that brings him joy is his daughter Glory, but when the family finds itself in need of money, she moves to Stockholm to look for a job. At first Jan is despondent, especially as Glory very quickly stops sending letters. But as time goes on, Jan begins to piece together what happened to Glory in Stockholm—though his conclusions differ wildly from everyone else’s.</p> <p>Blending family drama with social critique, <a href="https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/selma-lagerlof">Selma Lagerlöf</a> explores the ways in which community and generational relations can be affected by forces both beyond and within our control, and how redemption is possible, if we so choose.</p> <p>Lagerlöf considered titling the novel <i>A Swedish King Lear</i>, alluding to the generational conflicts central to both the novel and the play. Today <i>The Emperor of Portugallia</i> is considered a classic of Swedish literature, with multiple adaptations, including the now lost 1925 Hollywood film <i>The Tower of Lies</i> and a 1992 series for Swedish public television.</p></content>

		<content type="html"><p>William Thornton and Robert Seyd are two American friends who share an interest in mining. 		<summary type="text">An elderly Roman Stoic philosopher gives life advice to a young friend.</summary>
		<content type="html"><p><a href="https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/seneca">Seneca</a> was a Stoic philosopher and statesman in Rome’s early post-Augustan era. He was Nero’s tutor, and then his advisor when Nero became emperor in 54 CE. After Seneca retired from public life, he wrote a series of letters to his friend Lucilius, the procurator of Sicily. These letters were circulated right before Seneca’s death in 65 CE, when Nero forced him to commit suicide for his alleged involvement in a conspiracy.</p> <p>These letters, which were written for widespread publication as well as directly to Lucilius, mainly focus on guiding the reader to a life well-lived. At times, the advice is regarding specific personal issues, such as when he gives a review of a book written by Lucilius. Other letters give Seneca’s thoughts on broader issues like slavery, independence of thought, and virtue. Through all of them, his Stoicism shines through, whether in his metaphysics (like when he writes on “the god within us”) or in his focus on how virtue is the only good. His diverse interests are also on display, as when he addresses current events (like the burning of Lyons), or when he speculates on science (like when he offers his thoughts on animal instincts).</p> <p>These letters have been popular and influential since their initial circulation, and were widely read from the Roman period, up through the Middle Ages, and into the Renaissance, where <a href="https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/michel-de-montaigne">Michel de Montaigne</a> used them as a model for his <a href="https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/michel-de-montaigne/essays/charles-cotton"><i>Essays</i></a>. They remain highly regarded today for their practical and sage advice.</p></content>

		<content type="html"><p><i>Robur the Conqueror</i>, also published as <i>The Clipper of the Clouds</i>, opens in Philadelphia at a meeting of the Weldon Institute, a club of balloon enthusiasts. A stranger named Robur asks to address the members, then tells them that the future belongs to heavier-than-air machines. He mocks the club’s giant balloon, the <i>Go-Ahead</i>, and insults its members until the meeting erupts in chaos. 		<summary type="text">Driven by their shared idealism, two men returning to Imperial Russia to effect change face mortal danger from both an autocratic state desperate to preserve its power and a peasantry driven to desperation by centuries of servitude.</summary>
		<content type="html"><p>With <i>The Sowers</i>, a story ranging from the upper class drawing-rooms of London, Paris, and St. Petersburg to the vast estates and peasant villages of the Russian steppe, <a href="https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/henry-seton-merriman">Henry Seton Merriman</a> enjoyed his greatest popular success. Its protagonist is a young man of strong ideals and character who is known to his friends and London society as Paul Howard Alexis, to the vicious Russian aristocracy and the thousands of resentful peasants on his estate as Prince Pavlo Alexis, and to those same impoverished thousands as the “Moscow Doctor” sent by God, whose tireless, compassionate, selfless care sustains them. This enigmatic man is understood only by his closest advisor, friend, and confidant, Karl Steinmetz, a cosmopolitan utopian philosopher given to bouts of cynicism and sentimentalism. Together they resolve, come what may, to carry out the work of a charitable organization banned by the Russian state but crucial to the well-being of millions of oppressed peasants.</p> <p>The dangers are tremendous. The leadership of their organization is exiled by the Tsar’s secret police; nobles concerned with their peasants’ welfare are undermined by their peers; those same peasants, suspicious and superstitious, fear that anyone could be a spy or that any change in their lives will only deepen their misery; revolutionaries seek to exploit the growing unrest for their own political ends, while others seek to exploit it for their personal advantage. As Alexis and Steinmetz navigate this web of treachery, they realize that the greatest dangers and betrayals may come from those closest to them.</p> <p>In <i>The Sowers</i>, Merriman wrote with authority about the physical and political landscape of Russia, and with passion concerning those liberal ideals which became more evident in his later novels. For contemporary readers, the novel presented an exotic, mysterious place, the Russian Empire of the Romanovs, to which few traveled and which even fewer understood. As other European empires slowly changed and liberalized, Russia, with its vast spaces and rural millions, seemed increasingly anachronistic. Several of the more idealistic characters in the novel give voice to the author’s own sense that Russia would soon face an existential crisis when its peasantry finally rose up against those who had oppressed them for centuries, though the nature of such a revolution was unclear, and its trigger might not come in their lifetimes. For today’s reader, with the benefit of historical hindsight, those suggestions are uncannily prescient.</p> <p>Published in 1896, <i>The Sowers</i> anticipated the first Russian revolution by nine years. The extreme violence which attended the final fall of the Romanovs and their empire in 1917 occurred just fourteen years after Merriman’s own premature death in 1903.</p></content>

		<content type="html"><p>Two young couples, lost in an enchanted wood, are manipulated by quarreling fairies. A magician and his daughter entertain visitors he shipwrecked on their enchanted island. A king divides his lands unequally among his three daughters according to how well they flatter him. A witches’ prophecy sets a Scottish general on a tragic path.</p> <p><i>Beautiful Stories from Shakespeare</i> is a collection of retellings of twenty of <a href="https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/william-shakespeare">William Shakespeare’s</a> plays by noted children’s author <a href="https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/e-nesbit">E. Nesbit</a>. Each play is condensed to its core story and told using simple language that children can understand. While some quotations from Shakespeare are retained, the emphasis is on the stories rather than the language. The collection contains thirteen comedies and seven tragedies, but none of the histories.</p> <p>By 1907 Nesbit was well known for children’s novels such as <i><a href="https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/e-nesbit/five-children-and-it">Five Children and It</a></i> and <i><a href="https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/e-nesbit/the-railway-children">The Railway Children</a></i>. This collection expands on 1897’s <i>The Children’s Shakespeare</i>, which retells twelve of these plays. It follows in the tradition of prose retellings for children established by Charles and Mary Lamb’s 1807 <i>Tales from Shakespeare</i>.</p></content>

		<summary type="text">A German storm troop officer recounts his experiences in World War I.</summary>
		<content type="html"><p><a href="https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/ernst-junger">Ernst Jünger</a> was a German officer commanding storm troopers during World War I. This, his memoir of his time on the front, is one of the very first literary accounts of the Great War.</p> <p>Jünger begins his story as a private entering training in the Champagne region. He continues on to take part in various battles, climbing the ranks until attaining command of a regiment and accumulating fourteen different hits from bullets or shrapnel. His career ends near the very end of the war: his lung is punctured by a bullet while his men die all around him, and he’s sent to the rear to convalesce in the war’s waning months.</p> <p>The realities of this new style of war are described in a matter-of-fact and mostly apolitical way. Despite the obscene horrors Jünger graphically recounts, he seems stoic, even apathetic, about his role in the war, and about the destruction it caused. As he narrates battle after battle in gruesome detail, he falls back on a sense of “war without anger,” framing himself as a cog in an emotionless machine and his enemies as deserving of respect for their valor, and not hatred for their actions. Even as his superiors issue orders that he can clearly see will lead his men into the bloody meat grinder, Jünger remains obedient, patriotic, and driven by a sense of duty and national pride.</p> <p>The first edition was published in 1920, shortly after the war’s end. Jünger revised the book several times, transforming its raw diary style into a more literary one in 1924. Consequently, the book sold incredibly well, allowing Jünger to lead a post-war career as a writer. Its emphasis on nationalism made it a favorite of Nazi propagandists in the early 1930s, in contrast with <a href="https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/erich-maria-remarque">Erich Maria Remarque’s</a> equally matter-of-fact but more clearly anti-war <a href="https://standardebooks.org/ebooks/erich-maria-remarque/all-quiet-on-the-western-front/a-w-wheen"><i>All Quiet on the Western Front</i></a>, which the Nazis banned. Jünger, who was not a Nazi, again revised it in 1934 in an attempt to make it less attractive as nationalistic propaganda, but despite his attempts the book remained a popular one both with the Wehrmacht and with the public.</p></content>
